articles.title: ‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the Gallaghers
articles.summary: The crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride ever.
body: On 4 July last year, Oasis were all set to start the first gig of their hugely anticipated comeback, 16 years since the band imploded after Liam Gallagher swung a guitar in the direction of brother Noel’s head backstage in Paris. However, just 20 minutes before showtime, there was no sign of the singer. Some 74,500 fans in Cardiff’s Principality Stadium were going crazy, while Noel was left impatiently pacing around the venue’s loading bay, presumably wondering if everything was about to fall apart again.

The Cardiff entrance is one of the more dramatic scenes in Lovelace and co-director Dylan Southern’s film Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger, which briefly dwells on how the fractious working-class Manchester tearaways became the biggest rock band in the world in the 1990s before concentrating on how, 30 years later, they did it all again.

articles.title: Euro-Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch Program Launches at Iberseries & Platino Industria in Madrid (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: The Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid has launched the Euro-Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch Program, which assembles a cross-section of mainly European TV projects that seek to advance their development.
body: Backed by prominent production companies, the first edition has assembled a selection committee made up of seasoned professionals from the European audiovisual industry, including Laura Miñarro, VP of international business and coproduction at Buendía Estudios (Spain); Diego del Pozo, head of fiction at Atresmedia Televisión (Spain); José Fragoso, programming head at RTP1 and RTP Internacional (Portugal) and Georges Huercano, development and co-productions manager at RTL (Belgium).

“The first edition will bring together projects from Spain, Belgium, France, Portugal, Germany, Sweden, Finland, Canada and Uruguay, along with two invited projects thanks to collaboration agreements established with two of Europe’s leading markets and events specializing in series: Göteborg Film Festival, a key reference point for the Nordic audiovisual industry, and Seriencamp, one of the most relevant industry gatherings in Germany,” he noted.

The NFL has no shortage of elite quarterbacks. And most of them have never been to the Super Bowl.

On the opposite coast sits Justin Herbert of the Los Angeles Chargers. Widely regarded as one of the top ten quarterbacks in the league, he has yet to lead his team to a single postseason victory. We’ll see if Herbert can show up when it matters most.

articles.title: ‘The Burning Giants’ Review: An Arcane, Multi-Pronged Mystery About Ethnic Cleansing in Thailand
articles.summary: If it’s a bit too easy to group Thai director Phuttiphong Aroonpheng into a post-Apichatpong Weerasethakul wave of cryptic fablemakers, his latest only strengthens this association.
body: Almost a decade after his Orizzonti winner 'Manta Ray,' Phuttiphong Aroonpheng returns to the sidebar with an admirably elliptical but strangely single-note tale about the violent eviction and forced assimilation of an indigenous community.

In the beginning of “The Burning Giants,” a presumed-infected man named Yak (Awat Ratanapintha) scurries through a purgatorial hillside before being captured and detained by armed mountain police wearing gas masks. There’s a mysterious sickness going around, apparently caused by a toxic fog that invisibly burns the skin of whoever comes into contact with it. The indigenous man has some mild skin discoloration but it’s nothing like what’s happened to one of the cops’ own, whose raw, bubbling blisters are seen in agonizing close-up as he writhes in his cot back at the squad’s eerily vacant outpost.
points: If it’s a bit too easy to group Thai director Phuttiphong Aroonpheng into a post-Apichatpong Weerasethakul wave of cryptic fablemakers, his latest only strengthens this association.

articles.title: Do you know the lone, crying Oasis fan? The search is on by film-makers to find him
articles.summary: Filmmakers describe the gig as a "hugely emotional" experience that took Noel Gallagher by surprise.
body: The search is on for a lone and emotional Oasis fan featured in a film charting the brothers' comeback tour after the first gig in Cardiff, the directors have said.
Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern's portrayal of the band's world tour in 2025 also captured the moment Liam and Noel reunited in the rehearsal studios following a 15-year hiatus.

Reflecting on the opening gig at the Principality Stadium, Southern said: "That lad in particular is amazing because he's just had the experience of his life and he doesn't know what to do with it. And we want to find him."
He went on to say: "What it resulted in and what we didn't expect is a music documentary that's actually a feel-good film."

articles.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
articles.summary: Since beginning his second term, the US president has said he wanted to use the word 'America' to rename a lake, a gulf and even a US state.
body: The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.
"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.
Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.
The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.

articles.title: Company review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire tales
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men. Gather ye ’round the glowing screen for a Casey Affleck campfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes.
body: Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Nick Nolte is a hermit pining for his lost daughter, while Ben Mendelsohn plays a mean, mordant farmer who reaches for his handgun too readily. Both men, one suspects, are destined for a bloody end.

articles.title: Bunker review – Cruz and Bardem just can’t dig Florian Zeller’s shallow thriller out of a hole
articles.summary: Venice film festival: An architect (Javier Bardem) alienates his book editor wife (Penélope Cruz) when he agrees to build a luxurious bunker for a tech billionaire. Even the formidable pairing of Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem can’t save this new movie from writer-director Florian Zeller – his…
body: Bunker has nothing that interesting or original to say about its metaphorically showcased theme of alienation and inequality; the central relationship is left unexplored in favour of so-so home-invasion suspense styling – although one extended marital-argument scene showed what might have been achieved if their relationship was the film’s point – and the violent finale ending is outrageously glib, silly and unconvincing. An off-camera paramedic or doctor actually has to be heard explaining in a brief sentence afterwards what is supposed to have happened. Very lame.

Cruz and Bardem are Sofia and Miguel, a stylish Spanish couple with two teen daughters; the family has moved to London so that Sofia, a book editor, can take up a job managing a UK publisher’s foreign literature in translation list.

Miguel is a world-famous architect (what other sort is there?) who cordially tells an interviewer that he can work in any city. It seems as if he might himself have designed the huge, modernist rear extension to their handsome Victorian terrace house.

articles.title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
articles.summary: The comedian and Celebrity Traitors win big - see a full list of winners and nominees from the 26th edition of the awards.
body: Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian.

The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award.
Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends.
He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?"
